items.title: AI is automating most SRE incident responses but may reduce human expertise for handling complex failures, raising concerns about deskilling [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI isn't replacing SREs, it's deskilling them
items.summary:
A recent analysis highlights that while AI currently automates about 95% of routine incident responses in site reliability engineering (SRE), this shift may be deskilling human engineers by limiting their exposure to complex, novel failures. The article draws parallels to industrial automation's impact on blue-collar workers, where automation reduced hands-on practice and degraded critical intervention skills during rare crises.

Current AI applications in SRE include alert noise reduction, runbook execution for known issues, anomaly detection, and auto-remediation for common failures. Future developments aim to enhance multi-signal correlation, autonomous root-cause analysis, predictive incident detection, and AI-driven change risk assessments. However, as AI handles more routine tasks, human SREs may only engage with the most complex incidents, potentially eroding their intuition and expertise needed for effective response.

This trend raises questions about the long-term implications for SRE capabilities and system reliability, emphasizing the need to balance automation benefits with maintaining human skills essential for managing unprecedented outages.

items.title: Cisco president Jeetu Patel gives 27-year-old engineer unlimited AI tokens to rewrite legacy code, aiming to refactor 98% within 24 months [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Cisco gives engineer unlimited AI tokens to rewrite legacy code
items.summary:
Cisco president and chief product officer Jeetu Patel has empowered a 27-year-old engineer, Padmanabhan Krishnamurthy, with unlimited AI tokens to overhaul the company's legacy code. Krishnamurthy, a former startup founder acquired by Cisco, was previously underutilized but is now leading a project to refactor nearly all legacy code within two years.

Patel emphasizes the value of fresh perspectives from younger employees and seeks to recruit more young talent to challenge established practices. He encourages tension and collaboration between newer and veteran staff to foster innovation, viewing early-career workers as essential for injecting new ideas and driving transformation within the company.

items.title: Phorion detects persistent SSH backdoor in official Claude Code VS Code extension on Cursor Marketplace, prompting removal and incident response advisories
items.originalTitle: Backdoor in Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace
items.summary:
Phorion discovered a backdoor in the official Claude Code extension for Visual Studio Code distributed via the Cursor Marketplace, which installs a persistent SSH backdoor on macOS, Linux, and Windows systems. The compromised extension was removed from the marketplace and related registries after the discovery, and organizations using version 2.1.313 are urged to review their environments and engage incident response.

The backdoor operates by appending an attacker-controlled SSH public key to the authorized_keys file and attempts to enable SSH services on affected systems, though some platform-specific bugs limit its effectiveness, such as a macOS check that fails to enable Remote Login without root privileges. The extension runs malicious code immediately upon loading, granting attackers potential long-term interactive access to local files and developer tools without user interaction.

Despite some implementation errors that reduce impact on macOS and Windows, the malware remains a significant threat due to its persistence mechanisms and host reconnaissance capabilities. Users and administrators should monitor for signs of compromise and take appropriate remediation steps.

items.title: LRMoE introduces memory-aware load recalibration for efficient Mixture-of-Experts training on GPU nodes with limited memory, reducing training time by up to 44.8% [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LRMoE: Demand-Side Load Re-Calibration for Efficient MoE Training on Memory-Constrained Nodes
items.summary:
LRMoE is a new training system designed to optimize sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models on memory-constrained GPU nodes by recalibrating backward demand and balancing workload retention. It plans retention quotas and expert placement during forward execution and uses a load recalibration metric during backpropagation to select token-expert pairs within resource limits, reducing communication and computation overhead.

The system employs a capacity-aware routing algorithm and physical compaction techniques to minimize backward traffic and execution-buffer demand. Experiments on large-scale models Qwen3-30B-A3B and GLM4.5-106B-A12B demonstrate that LRMoE cuts cumulative MoE-layer training time to fixed-loss targets by 21.2% to 44.8% compared to existing methods like SYMI.

The system employs a capacity-aware routing algorithm and physical compaction techniques to minimize backward traffic and execution-buffer demand. Experiments on large-scale models Qwen3-30B-A3B and GLM4.5-106B-A12B demonstrate that LRMoE cuts cumulative MoE-layer training time to fixed-loss targets by 21.2% to 44.8% compared to existing methods like SYMI.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37720v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models offer scalable capacity for Web applications, but uneven routing creates computation and communication bottlenecks. Existing placement and replication methods redistribute this workload, yet additional expert copies compete with token-related buffers for limited GPU memory. We present LRMoE, a memory-aware MoE training system that jointly recalibrates backward demand and balances the retained workload. During forward execution, it plans retention quotas and expert placement under resource constraints while preserving all routed computations. During backpropagation, a load recalibration metric estimates each token-expert pair's contribution to the expert update and selects pairs within these quotas. A capacity-aware routing algorithm distributes retained pairs among eligible instances of their original experts. Physical compaction then forms smaller communication payloads and variable-size grouped GEMMs, reducing backward traffic, computation, and execution-buffer demand. Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and GLM4.5-106B-A12B show that LRMoE reduces cumulative MoE-layer training time to fixed-loss targets by 21.2-44.8% relative to SYMI.

items.title: Researchers develop amortized localized posterior inference method for model calibration, applying it to ocean turbulence closure to reduce predictive errors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Amortized Localized Posterior Inference for Model Calibration with Application to an Ocean Turbulence Closure
items.summary:
Researchers propose a method for model calibration that constructs localized posteriors by weighting observation likelihoods based on proximity to target contexts, accounting for uncertainties in observations and contexts. They use Gaussian localization weights with covariance inflation and approximate the posteriors via conditional normalizing flows through amortized variational inference. This approach integrates localized posteriors to produce marginalized parameter distributions, aiming to address model discrepancies across context domains.

In experiments with the Branin-Hoo model, the localized inference method reduced aggregate predictive errors compared to global posterior inference under both uniform and skewed context distributions. Applying the method to the k-ε turbulence closure in a single-column ocean model, with atmospheric surface forcing as context, showed that localized posterior calibration decreased temperature and zonal-velocity errors relative to deterministic and global-posterior calibration methods. The experiments were designed to allow local compensation, demonstrating the method's effectiveness in improving model calibration in complex physical systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model discrepancy may prevent a single calibration parameter from reproducing a physical response across the context domain. In addition, uncertainties in observations and contexts affect calibration and must be accounted for and quantified. We construct a family of localized posteriors by weighting observation likelihoods according to their proximity to a target context. Gaussian localization weights incorporate context uncertainty through covariance inflation, with reflection at domain boundaries and an optional correction for uneven context sampling. A conditional normalizing flow approximates the family of posteriors through amortized variational inference. Integrating the localized posteriors under a prescribed context measure gives the marginalized parameter distribution. In a twin experiment with the Branin-Hoo model, we compare global and localized inference under uniform and skewed context distributions. Localization reduces the reported aggregate predictive errors relative to the global posterior. An application to the k-$\epsilon$ turbulence closure in a single-column ocean model, with atmospheric surface forcing as context, shows that localized posterior calibration reduces temperature and zonal-velocity errors relative to deterministic and global-posterior calibration. Both twin experiments are constructed to admit local compensation.

items.title: ThinkJev introduces a hybrid system combining fast and slow reasoning for calibrated typed decisions, optimizing accuracy and computational cost on Qwen3.5 models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ThinkJev: One Thought, Every Budget for Calibrated Typed Decisions
items.summary: ThinkJev presents a method that uses a single language model to produce typed decisions either directly or after a reasoning step, balancing speed and accuracy. The system employs two modes: System 1 answers quickly using initial probabilities, while System 2 refines answers after additional thought, allowing adaptive computation based on confidence levels without extra training. Evaluations on Qwen3.5 models show that ThinkJev meets target error rates while reducing computation by selectively applying reasoning, achieving accuracy comparable to always thinking but with fewer thought tokens used. The approach was tested on JevBench, an independent typed-decision benchmark, where it performed similarly to existing thinking APIs, and the code and data are publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37732v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many uses of language models end in a typed decision: a choice among a closed set of options, whose probabilities code can act on. Reading those probabilities from one forward pass is fast but often wrong on decisions that take several steps, such as arithmetic, counting, and date comparison. Letting the model think first fixes most of these errors, but costs seconds per decision instead of milliseconds. To pay for thinking only where it helps, ThinkJev builds a fast and a slow system from one open hybrid-thinking model that can answer directly or after a thought. System 1 reads the model's probabilities for the option letters when it answers directly; System 2 reads the same letters after the model has thought on the same cached prompt, so escalating repeats no work and both systems give probabilities over the same options. Because the letters can be read after any number of thought tokens, one sampled thought also gives the answer under every thinking budget. Without training, ThinkJev lets System 1 answer alone only where a statistical test on labeled dev data guarantees that its accepted answers stay under a target error rate. At a 5% target, Qwen3.5-27B answers 24.5% of 8359 test decisions this way with a realized error of 3.9% (Qwen3.5-4B and 9B: 6.5% and 0.0%). For the rest, stopping each thought as soon as its answer is confident reaches 81.6% accuracy, against 82.7% for always thinking, with 72% of the thought tokens. Choosing when to think from System 1's confidence alone saves less, because the decisions System 1 is least sure of are often not the ones thinking fixes. On the public items of JevBench, an independent benchmark of typed-decision services, Qwen3.5-27B thinks on 29.4% and is not distinguishable in accuracy from the two thinking APIs listed (exploratory). Code and data generators are available at https://github.com/ding-xiaolu/ThinkJev.

items.title: OpenFrontiers releases a cross-disciplinary corpus of 12,151 open research problems and a benchmark of 200 math problems for evaluating scientific rediscovery by large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenFrontiers: A Collection of Open Research Problems and a Benchmark for Scientific Rediscovery
items.summary:
OpenFrontiers introduces a structured dataset combining over 12,000 open research problems with a benchmark of 200 recently resolved or still open mathematical problems, each formally verified and reviewed. The resource aims to facilitate evaluation of large language models (LLMs) on research-level problem solving by providing problem statements, context, progress, and formal proof verification under various conditions.

The benchmark includes a high-quality subset of 50 problems and uses an evaluation protocol with independent proof checkers in sandboxed environments under closed-book, frozen-retrieval, and live-web settings. Testing seven LLM agents showed that closed-book rediscovery of solutions is rare, while live-web success mainly reflects retrieval of existing published solutions. OpenFrontiers offers a foundation for measuring progress in scientific problem solving and is available on Hugging Face.

items.title: WebAnything launches automated framework to reconstruct reusable web environments from real URLs for scalable agent training and evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: WebAnything: From the Wild Web to Scalable Agent Environments
items.summary:
WebAnything introduces a fully automated system that creates source-grounded, reusable web environments from real URLs without requiring manual per-site engineering or repairs after initial setup. The framework uses an Explorer-Builder to collect browser-observable data and an independent verifier to ensure fidelity and guide repairs, enabling reproducible training and evaluation of web agents across diverse sites.

The team constructed 244 website artifacts spanning 14 application domains and 53 categories, supporting nearly 13,000 executed tasks. In a blind audit, WebAnything outperformed the human-assisted WebHarbor on three fidelity metrics. Fine-tuning the Qwen3.5-9B model on interaction trajectories collected by WebAnything improved success rates by up to 13.33 percentage points on standard benchmarks, demonstrating the framework's effectiveness for scalable web agent environments.

Human-assisted mirrors demand per-site engineering, while generative construction can diverge from specified real websites. Capture-and-replay preserves observations, with interaction coverage constrained by captured content and replay capabilities. We present WebAnything, a fully automated framework that reconstructs source-grounded, reusable Web environments from real URLs without per-site manual implementation or repair after initial setup and authorization. An Explorer-Builder collects browser-observable structures, resources, and interaction outcomes; an independent verifier checks frozen candidates and guides local repair or targeted source recapture. items.title: Study compares curated, LLM-generated, and data-derived ontologies as error checkers for LLM agents querying knowledge graphs, analyzing accuracy and false positives across public and private datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What Does an Ontology Catch? Curated, LLM-Generated and Data-Derived Ontologies as Checkers of LLM Agents over Knowledge Graphs
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated the effectiveness of different ontology sources—curated, generated by large language models (LLMs), and derived from data—in checking answers produced by LLM agents querying knowledge graphs. They tested these ontologies as prompt context, checkers, or both, across open-weight and proprietary agents on public graphs and a private graph with nearly one billion triples, measuring which errors were caught and which correct answers were wrongly flagged.

The study found that curated ontologies, such as the one used for UniProt, flagged more correct answers than LLM-derived or data-derived ontologies, but their precision was only slightly better than random. It also revealed that curated schemas can contradict their own data and that combining ontology sources or providing specific feedback to agents may influence error detection. These findings highlight limitations in relying solely on ontologies as reliable judges of LLM agent outputs over knowledge graphs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37809v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents that answer questions over Web knowledge graphs are increasingly wrapped in checks derived from the graph's ontology, on the assumption that a formal schema makes a reliable judge. Yet a checker can be wrong as well: it can miss errors, and it can flag correct answers and push the agent into "fixing" them. Whether a curated ontology is worth its cost as such a judge, and how it compares with an ontology an LLM writes or a schema mined from the data, is unknown. We make the checker itself the object of study. Across curated, LLM-generated and data-derived ontologies, used as prompt context, as a checker, or both, and across open-weight and proprietary agents on public graphs and a private graph of nearly $10^{9}$ triples, we account for what ontology-derived checks catch and what they wrongly flag. We show how each source trades caught errors against false alarms, how a curated schema used as published can contradict its own data, which errors structural checks miss, and whether combining sources or giving the agent the checker's specific feedback pays off. On UniProt, the curated ontology flags more correct answers than either an ontology derived from the data or one an LLM derives from a summary of the data with masked identifiers. On real agent answers, its flags are only marginally more precise than random flags.

items.title: Researchers measure where AI-written smart contracts lose intended behavior and propose an elicitation-first approach to recover missing requirements [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Measuring Where Intent Gets Lost in Agentic Smart Contract Synthesis
items.summary: Researchers studied the gap between AI-generated smart contract code and the intended behavior described in plain English, focusing on contracts that manage blockchain transactions and cannot be altered once deployed. They developed an evaluation method that compares the execution of AI-written contracts against original contracts by replaying transactions and measuring agreement, revealing that common evaluation tools miss many errors. The team introduced an elicitation-first architecture where AI agents ask clients clarifying questions before coding, check contracts against independently written executable answer keys, and report discrepancies instead of silently fixing code, which proved more effective than post-generation reviews or automated patches across multiple AI models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37830v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents can now write software from a plain-English description, but code that runs is not the same as code that does what was asked. This gap matters most for smart contracts, the programs behind Web3 applications that move money on a blockchain and cannot be fixed once deployed. We ask how to check whether an AI-written contract behaves as it should, and where the requested behavior gets lost. We design an evaluation built on execution rather than opinion. We replay the same transactions on an AI-written contract and on the original it should reproduce and measure how often they agree. We test every grading tool on planted mistakes, compare against an answer key written without the description, and audit our own scorer until known wrong answers cannot pass. Common methods, such as AI judges and standard analysis tools, miss obvious mistakes, and scoring choices matter too. Checking only the functions every system includes hid about half the difference between pipelines. We then propose an elicitation-first architecture. Before writing code, the agent asks the client a short checklist of questions, checks the contract against an independently written executable answer key, and returns disagreements to the client instead of silently rewriting code. Asking first matters far more than reviewing or patching afterwards, across three AI models, while automated security fixes often break requested behavior. A few well-chosen questions recover much of what a short description omits, and their value can be estimated without the original contract. To our knowledge, this is the first study in smart contract synthesis to gather missing requirements before generation and check the result against an independently written executable model. The lessons extend to any setting where AI agents turn requests into programs. We release our tools, 600 tasks and all results.

items.title: Researchers propose Partner-Outsider Positive Listening (PoPLi) to detect covert communication codes between AI agents by comparing behavioral responses to message rewording in simulated markets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Detecting Covert Collusion between AI Agents through Partner-Outsider Positive Listening
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Partner-Outsider Positive Listening (PoPLi), a behavioral test designed to detect secret communication codes between AI agents that appear as innocent messages. PoPLi measures the difference in how a partner agent using a code and an uninvolved agent respond to reworded messages with the same meaning, computed by replaying logged prompts. In simulated market experiments with various conditions, PoPLi reliably identified the presence of covert first-letter codes, while traditional message-only monitors failed to distinguish collusion scenarios.

The study tested five market conditions including no collusion, joint rewards with neutral or openly stated intentions, and covert codes with or without stated intentions. PoPLi values ranged from 0.48 to 0.59 when codes were present and near zero or negative without codes, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting private communication channels. However, PoPLi does not detect collusion based solely on incentives or codes embedded in message meaning, highlighting its specific focus on identifying covert signaling rather than collusion in general.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37849v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents that share a secret convention can coordinate through messages that look innocent, so a monitor that reads only the messages can miss them. We propose a behavioural test: a partner that uses a code reacts to the exact wording of a message, whereas an uninvolved agent placed in its seat does not. Partner--Outsider Positive Listening (PoPLi) is the difference between the two agents in how much their action changes when the message is reworded with its meaning kept, and it is computed after the fact by replaying logged prompts. In a simulated market with five conditions (no collusion, a joint reward with neutral messages, the same with an openly stated intention, a covert first-letter code, and the code with a stated intention), PoPLi is between 0.48 and 0.59 whenever the code is present (95% intervals all above 0.29) and between -0.10 and -0.01 without it. Message-only monitors did not separate the conditions: one reading the speaker's messages answered "no" in all 50 markets, and one reading every seller's messages flagged 9 of 10 markets with no collusion. PoPLi detects the use of a private channel, not collusion as such, and it cannot detect collusion through incentives alone or codes carried by meaning.

items.title: Researchers introduce LibStructBench to evaluate AI agents' ability to reconstruct sequencing-library structures and molecular workflows, finding current models struggle with exact molecular-state and workflow accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Evaluating and improving AI agents for sequencing protocol understanding
items.summary: Researchers have developed LibStructBench, a new benchmark designed to assess AI agents' capability to accurately reconstruct molecular structures and workflows from sequencing protocols, a key task for analyzing customized sequencing assays. Their experiments reveal that while leading AI agents often produce approximately correct reconstructions, they remain unreliable in achieving exact molecular-state representation and workflow connectivity. The study found that changing the underlying language model had a greater impact on performance than altering the agent framework, with significant differences observed only in molecular-state reconstruction. Additional knowledge improved recovery of oligo families in a small pilot but did not enhance overall molecular workflow scores. Attempts to autonomously accumulate procedural rules and cross-protocol examples resulted in inconsistent validation performance and no improvement in held-out molecular workflows, underscoring the need for more controlled and verifiable scientific reasoning methods in complex molecular protocol analysis.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37851v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing scientific-agent benchmarks rarely evaluate whether agents can reconstruct the exact molecular structures and generation workflows specified by sequencing protocols, a capability critical for analyzing customized sequencing assays. We introduce LibStructBench, a document-grounded benchmark for reconstructing sequencing-library structures and molecular workflows. Our experiments show that frontier agents often produce approximately correct reconstructions but remain unreliable at exact reconstruction, particularly in molecular-state representation and workflow connectivity. Switching the underlying language model produced larger average performance differences than switching agent harnesses, with a statistically significant difference only for molecular-state reconstruction. Additional knowledge improved oligo-family recovery in a small pilot without improving mean molecular-workflow scores. Autonomous accumulation of procedural rules and cross-protocol examples showed non-monotonic validation performance and no mean held-out molecular-workflow improvement in the tested trajectory. These findings highlight the need for more controlled and verifiable approaches to scientific reasoning about molecular processes in complex experimental protocols.

items.originalTitle: Seq@K: Evaluating Language Models Under Sequential Feedback
items.summary: Researchers propose Seq@K, an evaluation method that tests whether language models can solve problems within K sequential attempts using feedback after each failure, addressing limitations of existing metrics like Pass@K. They evaluated Seq@K across seven benchmarks and sixteen models, finding it reveals different model rankings and more efficient configurations compared to traditional metrics. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37859v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language-model agents differ fundamentally from prior intelligent systems in their ability to learn from natural language in context. This capability enables agents to iteratively refine their answers in response to feedback, a prevalent mode of operation in modern agentic workflows. However, the community primarily ranks models by metrics such as Pass@1 or Pass@K, which cannot capture how they utilize feedback on prior attempts. We introduce Seq@K, a natural evaluation protocol that measures whether a model can solve a problem within K sequential attempts, provided feedback after each previous failure. Unlike multi-turn agentic benchmarks that examine long-horizon planning, Seq@K isolates and formalizes the core capability of refinement from feedback. We evaluate Seq@K on a suite of 7 benchmarks and 16 frontier models, and show that Seq@K reveals a materially different model-selection landscape: under Seq@K, (1) model rankings often differ, (2) the Pareto frontiers admit more efficient configurations and (3) the gains from choosing the optimal model configuration can widen or shrink relative to those of Pass@K. We further show that analyzing model trajectories under Seq@K helps characterize iterative refinement behavior, such as the rate at which models address issues raised in feedback, or how rigidly they hold onto their own answers. Finally, we study how the nature of feedback affects models' iterative refinement, showing that practitioners must carefully design and benchmark the feedback loops of iterative agentic systems. Together, these results establish how Seq@K offers a more faithful metric for intelligent systems that typically operate in such feedback loop, and the necessity to consider Seq@K in evaluating models for these systems.

items.title: Researchers analyze visual representations of Indian cuisine to assess food similarity beyond identity using multiple pretrained models and an expanded Khana dataset [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What Constitutes Food Similarity? Visual Representations and Retrieval in Indian Cuisine
items.summary:
Researchers studied how different visual representations organize Indian foods into relational neighborhoods, revealing or obscuring culinary relationships beyond simple identity preservation. They used seven pretrained models, including convolutional, transformer-based, self-supervised, and image-text aligned models, to evaluate image-to-image retrieval and image-to-dish neighborhoods, focusing on culinary-family structure and cross-representation agreement.

The study found substantial variation in image-level neighborhoods across representations, including similarities crossing culinary-family boundaries. Aggregated dish-level visual similarity showed common structure despite local variation but correlated less strongly with recipe-derived similarity. These results indicate that food similarity depends on representation, modality, and abstraction level, suggesting that recognition performance alone cannot capture relational structure and that understanding these factors is essential for integrating multiple food information modalities into a coherent similarity framework.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37867v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Food similarity underlies retrieval, recommendation, substitution, and other food computing tasks, yet food representations are typically evaluated by identity preservation. We ask what happens to food similarity beyond identity: how different visual representations organize foods into relational neighborhoods, what culinary relationships these neighborhoods reveal or obscure, and how consistently these structures emerge across representations. Indian cuisine provides a challenging setting in which visually similar foods may have different culinary identities, while foods within a culinary family can vary substantially in appearance. Using an expanded Khana dataset and seven pretrained visual representations spanning convolutional, transformer-based, self-supervised, and image-text aligned models, we evaluate image-to-image retrieval and image-to-dish neighborhoods, examining culinary-family structure, contrast cases, and cross-representation agreement. We also aggregate image representations to compare dish-level visual similarity across models and against recipe-derived similarity for the same dishes. Image-level neighborhoods vary substantially across representations, including similarities across culinary-family boundaries. At the dish level, aggregation reveals common visual structure despite local variation, but this structure corresponds less strongly with recipe-derived similarity. These findings show that recognition performance alone cannot characterize relational structure: food similarity depends on representation, modality, and abstraction level rather than being a fixed property of the food collection. Understanding these structures is therefore a prerequisite to combining multiple food information modalities into a coherent notion of similarity.

items.title: Verification Learning Theory models how perceived AI assistant reliability affects evidence checking and rule retention in AI-assisted judgment tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Verification Learning Theory: A Process Model of Checking and Retention in AI-Assisted Judgment
items.summary:
Verification Learning Theory (VLT) proposes a process model linking perceived reliability of AI assistance to the frequency of evidence checking and subsequent retention of decision rules in independent judgment. The theory predicts that perceiving AI as fallible can improve delayed unaided judgments by encouraging more checking, even without observed errors, but this benefit disappears when checking is already mandatory and performed.

The model assumes that learning depends solely on checking behavior and that each genuine check contributes equally to rule retention. Simulations explore the model's implications and parameter sensitivities, while comparisons with other cognitive theories highlight where predictions differ or align. The framework also outlines experiments to test the mechanism and distinguishes between retaining practiced rules and recognizing which rule applies to new claims.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37875v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate AI assistance can improve immediate judgments while reducing opportunities to practise the operations needed for independent performance. Verification Learning Theory (VLT) formalises this possibility for claim-evaluation practice followed by correct, independent, rule-specific feedback. The model links perceived assistant reliability to evidence checking and links the history of those checks to retained rule use. Its strict form assumes that task demands and perceived reliability influence learning only through checking, with equal learning per genuine check. It therefore predicts that perceived fallibility can improve delayed unaided judgment even without observed assistant errors, and that this advantage disappears when checking is already required and performed. Rule-specific gains and forecasts from checking histories provide further tests. Simulations examine the consequences and parameter dependence of these commitments; they do not constitute empirical validation. Comparisons with depth-of-processing and feedback-encoding accounts identify where predictions diverge and where the accounts remain observationally equivalent. The framework specifies experiments that can test the proposed mechanism and separates retention of practised rules from the broader problem of recognising which rule applies to a new claim.

items.title: Researchers analyze when and how socio-demographic information improves pluralistic offensiveness modeling, highlighting the role of explicit reasoning in enhancing prediction accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Anatomy of Socio-Demographics in Pluralistic Offensiveness Modeling: When and Where It Helps, and the Role of Reasoning
items.summary: This study examines the impact of incorporating annotators' socio-demographic data into pluralistic offensiveness models, addressing mixed prior findings by analyzing effectiveness and mechanisms across three multi-annotator datasets using large language models. The researchers find that demographic information yields small, inconsistent gains at the individual level but clearer benefits when aggregated at group and population levels, as aggregation reduces individual variation that obscures demographic signals. They also show that explicit reasoning, which separates baseline judgments from demographic-specific deviations, improves both baseline estimation and demographic shifts, leading to better final predictions compared to direct demographic conditioning. These results suggest that the value of socio-demographic information depends on evaluation methods and model guidance, explaining previous inconsistent evidence.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37896v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Subjective judgments such as offensiveness often vary substantially across individuals, motivating pluralistic modeling approaches that incorporate annotators' socio-demographic information to capture this variation. However, prior findings on the benefits of socio-demographic information for pluralistic modeling are mixed, calling for a systematic analysis of both its effectiveness and the mechanisms through which it improves prediction. In this work, we study $\textbf{when}$ and $\textbf{where}$ socio-demographics benefit pluralistic offensiveness modeling, as well as $\textbf{the role of explicit reasoning}$ in leveraging this information. Across three multi-annotator datasets with prompted and trained LLMs, we first show that demographic gains are small and inconsistent for individual predictions but become clearer at the group and population levels, because aggregation attenuates the idiosyncratic variation that masks small but systematic demographic signals. Second, using a reasoning and prediction format that explicitly decomposes individual judgment into an overall baseline and a demographic-specific deviation, we show that the gains arise from both components: demographic information improves baseline estimation and enables meaningful demographic-specific shifts, and interventions show that better component estimates improve final predictions. Finally, comparing direct demographic conditioning with explicit reasoning about how the text interacts with annotator demographics, we find that reasoning yields more accurate baseline and shift estimates as well as final predictions, whereas conditioning alone rarely produces informative shifts. These results suggest that the mixed evidence in prior work may partly stem from individual-level evaluation, and that the value of socio-demographic information depends on both how it is evaluated and how models are guided to use it.

items.title: Researchers introduce FilingLoop, a self-evolving LLM agent framework and benchmark for reviewing and revising corporate disclosures using SEC correspondence from 96 companies [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision
items.summary:
FilingLoop is an interactive benchmark and agent framework designed to support language model agents in reviewing and revising corporate disclosures by identifying deficiencies, acquiring missing facts, and verifying revisions against evidence-backed requirements. It reconstructs 380 IPO review tasks from historical SEC correspondence and evaluates filings against over 6,000 requirements, auditing unsupported claims and harmful revisions.

The framework enables iterative review and revision within cases and procedural learning across cases without updating model weights, allowing adaptation to be assessed on new tasks. In evaluations, FilingLoop improved requirement fulfillment from 24.28% to 27.96% and full comment resolution from 16.90% to 20.75%, with a modest increase in cost compared to a fixed policy. This approach links discovered concerns, company facts, and committed revisions, providing detailed feedback to improve future review procedures.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37905v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Public disclosure repositories such as SEC EDGAR support informed investment through web access to corporate filings. Supporting their review with language model agents requires discovering unstated deficiencies across related documents, acquiring missing company facts, and verifying that requested revisions satisfy evidence-backed requirements. Existing financial question-answering evaluations provide limited evidence of these interactive capabilities. We introduce \textbf{FilingLoop}, an interactive benchmark and a self-evolving agent framework for corporate disclosure review and revision. Grounded in historical U.S.\ Securities and Exchange Commission correspondence, FilingLoop reconstructs 380 predominantly IPO review tasks from 96 companies under distinct information constraints. An evaluator separate from the acting agents scores final filings and responses against 6,099 eligible requirements and audits unsupported claims and harmful revisions. Our framework couples iterative review and revision within each case with procedural learning across cases, converting requirement-level evaluation feedback into role-specific guidance without updating model weights. Updates affect only subsequent cases, allowing procedural adaptation to be assessed without retrying scored tasks. On the evaluated stream, evolution increases requirement fulfillment from 24.28\% to 27.96\% and full comment resolution from 16.90\% to 20.75\%, with a 5.8\% increase in total cost over the fixed-policy variant. FilingLoop connects the concerns an agent discovers with the company facts it obtains and the revisions it commits, providing requirement-level feedback for procedures used in later review tasks.

items.title: Researchers introduce HRF-Res, a spiking reservoir computing model using frequency-selective Harmonic Resonate-and-Fire neurons to improve classification accuracy and energy efficiency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Low-Pass Dynamics: Frequency-Selective Spiking Reservoirs with Resonant Neurons
items.summary: Researchers have developed HRF-Res, a liquid state machine that replaces traditional Leaky Integrate-and-Fire neurons with Harmonic Resonate-and-Fire neurons exhibiting intrinsic oscillatory dynamics. This design enables the reservoir to selectively respond to input frequencies, capturing frequency-specific temporal patterns and improving classification accuracy without compromising energy efficiency. Evaluated on ten benchmarks including time series, sequential images, audio spike trains, and neuromorphic vision, HRF-Res achieved state-of-the-art accuracy among spiking reservoir methods while consuming up to 19 times less energy than comparable non-spiking oscillatory reservoirs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37906v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spiking reservoir computing combines the training efficiency of fixed recurrent reservoirs with the energy efficiency of event-driven inference, where computation is triggered by sparse spikes rather than executed densely at every timestep. However, existing spiking reservoirs almost exclusively rely on Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons, whose low-pass dynamics limit their ability to distinguish information encoded at different temporal frequencies. We introduce HRF-Res, a liquid state machine in which LIF neurons are replaced by a heterogeneous population of Harmonic Resonate-and-Fire (HRF) neurons. These neurons exhibit intrinsic oscillatory dynamics and selectively respond to input frequencies, enabling the reservoir to capture frequency-specific temporal patterns. The result is more discriminative representations and higher classification accuracy than LIF-based reservoirs, achieved without sacrificing the energy efficiency of spiking computation, with up to 19x lower energy consumption than an equivalent non-spiking oscillatory reservoir. Evaluated on ten benchmarks spanning time series, sequential images, audio spike trains, and neuromorphic vision, HRF-Res achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among spiking reservoir methods. These results demonstrate that introducing frequency-selective dynamics into spiking reservoirs improves representational quality and classification performance while preserving their inherent energy efficiency.

items.title: Researchers introduce SciGame benchmark for evaluating scientific discovery agents using real and counterfactual environments with historical and temporal scientific laws [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SciGame: Let Agents Play the Scientific Discovery Games in the Real and Counterfactual World
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SciGame, a controlled benchmark that transforms scientific literature into structured scientific cards, each providing paired original and counterfactual environments for testing AI agents in scientific discovery tasks. SciGame includes a historical collection of canonical laws and a temporal collection from recent papers, evaluating agents under various protocols in identification and discovery settings.

Experiments with five advanced models revealed that familiar priors can hinder performance when underlying relations change, adaptive experimentation benefits stronger models but can harm weaker ones under limited resources, and accurate explanations may mask quantitative errors. While current agents can actively investigate systems, accurately inducing exact symbolic laws in new contexts remains a significant challenge.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37919v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly used for scientific discovery. However, existing benchmarks mix law inference with programming, score data fitting instead of prediction on unseen inputs, and do not separate empirical evidence from pretrained priors. We introduce SciGame, a controlled benchmark that converts scientific literature into structured scientific cards. Each card yields a pair of Original and dimensionally consistent Counterfactual environments with the same task interface. SciGame contains a Historical collection of canonical laws and a live Temporal collection curated from papers published after model knowledge cutoffs. It evaluates agents in candidate-guided Identification and open-ended Discovery settings. Each setting runs under Prior-only, Fixed, and Adaptive protocols. Experiments on five frontier models yield three findings. First, familiar priors hurt performance once the governing relation is altered. Second, adaptive experimentation helps the strongest models but harms weaker ones under limited budgets. Third, good explanations can hide quantitative failures. Recovering the exact symbolic form remains the main bottleneck, even when agents interpret evidence correctly. Current agents can investigate systems actively, but inducing exact laws in unfamiliar settings remains an open challenge.

items.title: VerifiedLab: Harnessing Knowns for Unknowns [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: VerifiedLab: Harnessing Knowns for Unknowns
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37923v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Across human history, knowledge has undergone several transitions, from orality to writing and then to digital archives. At each transition, humans established new conventions to preserve knowledge for the new era. Nowadays, as research agents are increasingly deployed for laboratory experiments, knowledge is crossing another boundary: from records written for humans to those for machines. In this work, we introduce VerifiedLab, a multi-agent harness framework for this human-to-machine transition of knowledge. VerifiedLab transforms research output from passive artifacts into active systems that accelerate downstream use, adoption and prediction of future trends. In VerifiedLab, a team of AI scientists with distinct roles reasons over records verified field by field: a principal investigator plans, a librarian computes the evidence directly from the records, specialists draft, and a gate and a critic check each claim against the measured reliability of its data before the harness decides whether to release or withhold it. We demonstrate the efficacy of VerifiedLab through extensive experiments on perovskite solar cells: VerifiedLab recovers known physical trends, anticipates devices reported a year later, and lets AI scientists inherit the literature together with a measure of how far it can be trusted. By scaling the inference-time verification compute, VerifiedLab introduces a new pathway for knowledge dissemination and machine harness for AI co-scientists.

items.title: GARDEN: Generalist Autonomous Reward Design Through Evidence Navigation for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: GARDEN: Generalist Autonomous Reward Design Through Evidence Navigation for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37926v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables teams of agents, such as robots and autonomous vehicles, to learn coordinated behavior, but what such teams learn is largely determined by their reward function. Because task success alone provides too little guidance for learning, intermediate rewards are usually designed by hand, and this effort must often be repeated whenever the environment or the team changes. Large language models (LLMs) can automate the effort by writing reward functions as code, yet the resulting rewards are typically designed and tested in a single setting. To enable their reuse across settings, GARDEN (Generalist Autonomous Reward Design through Evidence Navigation) is proposed, in which one reward program is developed for a family of related scenarios and transferred, unchanged, to scenarios that were not available during its design. During development, environment code, training records, and agent behavior are investigated by an LLM reward engineer, and draft rewards are tested in trial training runs, while the learning algorithm and the rule for selecting the final reward are held fixed. On unseen scenarios of the Overcooked and SMAX benchmarks, task returns were increased by 58.2% and 52.5% over the default rewards on two kitchen layouts, and the mean win rate in two combat scenarios was raised from 51.0% to 89.9%. Under matched candidate and probe budgets, this exceeded the 84.2% and 79.2% obtained with fixed diagnostic feedback and Eureka-inspired reward reflection. These results show that a single autonomously engineered reward can be reused effectively across related cooperative scenarios.

items.title: Understanding Large Language Models as Numerical Optimizers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Understanding Large Language Models as Numerical Optimizers
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37932v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as potential tools for numerical optimization. Despite promising results, their intrinsic optimization capabilities and limitations remain poorly understood, particularly in high dimensions. This paper investigates the ability of LLMs to exploit mathematical problem structures and generate feasible, near-optimal solutions. We develop an evaluation framework that distinguishes solution quality from execution failures, including numerical inaccuracies, constraint violations, and output-format errors. Using representative problems from convex optimization, fractional programming, and constrained projection, we assess LLM performance against deterministic reference solvers across different dimensions. Our results reveal that LLMs can capture useful optimization structures and produce near-optimal solutions, even when their outputs fail to satisfy numerical or formatting requirements. However, reliability deteriorates with increasing problem dimension and depends strongly on the underlying optimization structure. To further investigate the limitations, we deploy an iterative refinement mechanism that provides targeted feedback on feasibility and solution quality. The results demonstrate that iterative refinement substantially improves reliability and extends the range of problem dimensions over which LLMs produce valid solutions. Nevertheless, persistent numerical and structural errors limit their applicability as standalone optimizers. These findings provide insights into the capacity and limits of LLM-based optimization and motivate hybrid approaches that combine LLM reasoning with deterministic numerical verification.

items.title: SkillMem: Compact External Skill Memory for Latent Multi-Agent Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SkillMem: Compact External Skill Memory for Latent Multi-Agent Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Latent multi-agent systems reduce inference cost by keeping intermediate reasoning and inter-agent communication in continuous representations.\ Reusable skills, however, are commonly supplied as text or stored as layer-wise Key-Value states or skill-specific model parameters, introducing repeated processing or substantial per-skill storage.\ We introduce \textbf{SkillMem}, which represents each reusable skill as a small external latent memory and makes it directly available during latent multi-agent reasoning.\ A role-conditioned cross-attention reader allows the same memory to guide different agents according to their roles and current hidden states.\ We train the skill memories and shared reader through behavioral distillation, matching the change in token predictions induced by a textual skill while keeping the backbone frozen.\ For our experiments, we obtain textual skills from paired successful and failed multi-agent trajectories, although existing skills can also be compiled directly.\ Across six benchmarks and Qwen3 models ranging from 4B to 14B parameters, SkillMem provides strong gains for smaller backbones while preserving efficient latent multi-agent inference across model scales.\ We use the same $8\times256$ memory configuration across all evaluated model scales, requiring 9.6\,KB of skill-specific storage per skill, including its retrieval embedding.\ For a library of 100 skills, SkillMem reduces total storage by more than $38\times$ compared with alternative skill representations and achieves up to a $4.23\times$ end-to-end inference speedup.\ These results show that compact procedural memories can be reused without sacrificing the efficiency of latent multi-agent reasoning.

items.originalTitle: GAUSS: A Workload-Aware Analytical and Monte-Carlo Simulator for LLM Inference Serving
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference has become an operational workload that fleets must provision, monitor, and bill against latency service-level objectives (SLOs). A single throughput number cannot answer the questions operators actually face, because generative serving couples two phases with very different service characteristics, continuous batching reshapes the effective service process, and user-visible tail latency can degrade long before aggregate throughput saturates. We present GAUSS, a workload-aware analytical and Monte-Carlo simulator that predicts the full distributions of time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-between-tokens (TBT), together with the sustainable request rate, for a given workload, engine, and accelerator. GAUSS pairs calibrated, phase-specific latency surfaces for prefill and decode with a Lindley-recurrence model of queueing under stochastic arrivals and estimates performance by ensemble Monte-Carlo sampling rather than by replaying a single trace. This lets GAUSS reason about workloads, routing policies, and hardware that have never been deployed, and to capture the latency tails that trace-driven simulators systematically under-sample. We describe the model and show how it supports operating-point selection, traffic segmentation, and shortest-remaining-processing-time scheduling capacity questions that trace-driven simulators cannot address.

items.title: Algorithmic Bias from the Perspectives of Healthcare Professionals [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Algorithmic Bias from the Perspectives of Healthcare Professionals
items.summary: arXiv:2610.38006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper focuses on algorithmic bias of machine learning and artificial intelligence applications in healthcare information systems. Based on the quantitative data and qualitative comments from a survey and interviews with healthcare professionals, who have different job roles (e.g., clinical vs. administrative), this study provides findings about the relationships between algorithmic bias, perceived fairness, and the intended acceptance and adoption of ML algorithms and algorithm generated outcomes. The results suggest that the opinions of healthcare professionals toward the causes of algorithmic bias, the criteria of algorithm assessment, the perceived fairness, and bias mitigation approaches may vary depending on their job roles, perspectives, tasks, and the algorithm characteristics. More research is needed to investigate algorithmic bias to ensure fairness and equality in healthcare.

items.title: Assessing Language Models for Scientific Applications: Inertial Confinement Fusion as a Use Case [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Assessing Language Models for Scientific Applications: Inertial Confinement Fusion as a Use Case
items.summary: arXiv:2610.38024v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Advancing language models for specialized scientific applications requires evaluations of scientific fluency, physical reasoning, and quantitative analyses. Using inertial confinement fusion (ICF) as a test case, we have developed an expert-curated benchmark of 250 questions spanning qualitative reasoning, numerical calculation, symbolic derivation, and equation formulation. Responses have been evaluated using deterministic numerical and symbolic checks together with language-model judges. We compared a variety of out-of-the-box closed-source and open-source large language models with Prospero, a model specialized through combined domain-adaptive pretraining and supervised fine-tuning for ICF. We also conducted initial retrieval-assisted evaluations. Prospero improved its aggregate score by 10.7 percentage points over its base model, with gains across all question types. Frontier models achieved the highest aggregate scores, but critical physics errors persisted, particularly in numerical calculations. We note that domain-specific performance can improve through specialization, but benchmark gains alone do not establish scientific reliability. Retrieval improved performance for a smaller model but yielded no statistically significant improvement for a frontier model. Two scientific stress tests further illustrate useful capabilities and the need for expert assessment of physical assumptions and model validity. Based on these findings, we recommend evaluating existing domain capabilities and retrieval benefits before committing to substantial additional specialization.

items.title: PromptSense: Sentiment-Aware Mental Health Chatbot with Dynamic Prompting [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: PromptSense: Sentiment-Aware Mental Health Chatbot with Dynamic Prompting
items.summary: arXiv:2610.38044v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Current Large Language Models (LLMs)-based mental health chatbots often lack sufficient empathy, contextual awareness, and safety mechanisms, potentially leading to ineffective or harmful interactions. This paper proposes a novel framework that integrates sentiment and depression analysis with a rule-based filtering mechanism prior to model inference. By dynamically constructing prompts based on emotional and risk-related insights, the framework aims to significantly improve the contextual relevance, empathy, and risk-aware of model-generated responses. We evaluated four model strategies and two prompt engineered variants across qualitative metrics such as empathy, helpfulness, clarity, relevance, safety, as well as toxicity assessments using the Perspective API. Experimental results indicate that the prompt engineering approaches outperforms DSFT and RLAIF by 1.8\% and 1.1\% respectively.

items.title: Evaluating Causal Reasoning in LLMs: A Case Study in the Challenges of Procedural Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Evaluating Causal Reasoning in LLMs: A Case Study in the Challenges of Procedural Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.38100v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) appear to represent and reason about a large range of phenomena. In particular, recent studies have examined whether LLMs can accurately reason about causation. One of the most commonly used benchmarks for evaluating formal causal reasoning in LLMs is CLadder, a framework for procedural generation of benchmark data sets that was released in 2023. Experiments with CLadder appear to indicate that LLMs can perform formal causal reasoning in a large percentage of generated examples. In this paper, we examine what can be reliably inferred when LLMs perform well on test sets produced by CLadder. We identify several examples of superficial and highly predictive patterns that the CLadder generator embeds in data sets it generates. We find that even simple models such as random forests perform well on CLadder-generated data sets after training on a sample of generated data. We also find that the performance of many commercial LLMs on CLadder test sets is extremely brittle and that removing large sections of the text that are critical for formal causal reasoning has almost no effect on performance. Given these results, the most likely hypothesis for the strong performance of state-of-the-art LLMs on CLadder is that they are exploiting superficial patterns learned from exposure to training data from the generator. Any inference that LLMs are exhibiting more complex causal reasoning must rule out this hypothesis.

items.title: AI-Driven Digital Twin Framework for Warehouse Logistics Automation Optimization [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI-Driven Digital Twin Framework for Warehouse Logistics Automation Optimization
items.summary: arXiv:2610.38101v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In recent years, warehouse logistics optimization has increasingly focused on intelligent, data-driven systems to enhance operational efficiency. Conventional static product placement strategies are being progressively replaced by dynamic slotting approaches that can adapt to real-time variations in warehouse conditions. In this work, we present a novel framework that employs a reinforcement learning agent integrated within a FlexSim-based Digital Twin environment for real-time product placement optimization. The proposed agent continuously learns from streaming operational data, enabling it to reduce picking time while improving overall system throughput. The simulation environment models a four-zone warehouse layout with forklift-based material handling and leverages the Asset Administration Shell framework to ensure seamless interaction between the learning agent, physical asset, and the digital twin. Experimental evaluation demonstrates substantial performance gains, with the proposed approach achieving a 29.66\% reduction in average picking time, a 35.42\% increase in throughput, and an 18.54\% decrease in travel distance.

items.title: Too Hard, Too Easy, Just Right: Performance-Driven Challenge Adaptation in Virtual Reality Firefighter Training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Too Hard, Too Easy, Just Right: Performance-Driven Challenge Adaptation in Virtual Reality Firefighter Training
items.summary: arXiv:2610.38117v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective firefighter training requires practice under dynamic and stressful emergency conditions, yet real-world live-fire exercises are costly, risky, and difficult to scale. Virtual Reality (VR) offers a safe and controllable alternative, but many existing VR firefighter training systems rely on fixed scenarios or provide limited difficulty adaptation, making it difficult to maintain an appropriate level of challenge for skill development as trainees' performance changes over time. To address this limitation, we present ProACT, a performance-driven adaptive training system that regulates scenario difficulty through closed-loop interactions between trainee performance and simulated fire dynamics. Specifically, ProACT combines a global module that continuously adjusts scene-level fire spread dynamics in real time based on trainee performance with a local module that periodically updates object-level flammability across the environment. Our evaluation shows that ProACT improves both objective training performance and subjective user experience compared with existing adaptive and non-adaptive baselines. We further discuss how adaptive immersive environments can extend beyond firefighting to broader training domains.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.38117v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective firefighter training requires practice under dynamic and stressful emergency conditions, yet real-world live-fire exercises are costly, risky, and difficult to scale. Virtual Reality (VR) offers a safe and controllable alternative, but many existing VR firefighter training systems rely on fixed scenarios or provide limited difficulty adaptation, making it difficult to maintain an appropriate level of challenge for skill development as trainees' performance changes over time. To address this limitation, we present ProACT, a performance-driven adaptive training system that regulates scenario difficulty through closed-loop interactions between trainee performance and simulated fire dynamics. Specifically, ProACT combines a global module that continuously adjusts scene-level fire spread dynamics in real time based on trainee performance with a local module that periodically updates object-level flammability across the environment. Our evaluation shows that ProACT improves both objective training performance and subjective user experience compared with existing adaptive and non-adaptive baselines. We further discuss how adaptive immersive environments can extend beyond firefighting to broader training domains.

items.title: Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON
items.summary: arXiv:2610.38120v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) treat all context tokens uniformly, lacking explicit separation between executable instructions and passive data. This leads to prompt injection vulnerabilities, ambiguous instruction binding, and unreliable execution control. We present a post-training methodology using LLMON (LLM Object Notation), a framework that enables separating instructions from data and requires explicit identifier-based execution. We construct a large-scale structured training corpus of 4.6B tokens spanning general, RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), and tool-calling data, augmented with distractor-infused variants in which competing instructions and irrelevant data segments are present in context but not referenced. Post-training two Granite-4.1 base models (3B and 8B) through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning, we show that LLMON-structured supervision reduces attack success rates on indirect prompt-injection benchmarks from 53-100% to 0.02-5.6% while preserving general capabilities. We further introduce attention-based interpretability metrics that diagnose failure modes at individual transformer layers for structured inputs, revealing how our approach reshapes internal attention patterns. Our results demonstrate that explicit execution semantics can be taught through standard post-training without architectural modification.

items.title: Decompose, Don't Expand: Capability-Independent AI Systems by Construction [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Decompose, Don't Expand: Capability-Independent AI Systems by Construction
items.summary: arXiv:2610.38144v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A recurring design choice in building AI systems is whether, when a task is too hard for a model, to expand the model (make it larger, better-prompted, fine-tuned), or to decompose the task (extract the parts that admit a deterministic solution to a host, leaving the model only the irreducibly fuzzy residue). We make three claims. First, that many tasks commonly delegated whole to a model are in fact deterministic tasks with a small generative core. Second, and our central empirical result, that decomposing such a task yields a measurable and desirable property we call parity by construction: on the extracted sub-tasks the model-size performance curve becomes flat, because no model performs them at all. We measure this across nine models spanning a 494M-parameter local checkpoint to a frontier Opus-class model, a thirty-fold parameter range on the local family alone: once the host resolves the context, operation selection scores identically for all nine models and selector resolution for eight of nine, while the one task that does not decompose, labelling, remains sloped across the same range. Because the task leaves the model, a stock checkpoint suffices: no task-specific training and no fine-tuning. Third, that this is a general design discipline, not a domain trick: we show the same move recurring across physics setup, motion retargeting, and object-model editing, and in a Web-CLI tool family (same author, so not an independent replication). We give a method for locating the cut, the construction that makes a cut exist (a deterministic surface and a closed grammar over it), and a way to make the residue safe (resolve the deterministic context; verify the generative output), position the work against neuro-symbolic AI, tool-augmented language models, and generate-and-verify approaches, and are explicit about what is measured (one domain) versus illustrative (the rest).

items.title: SkillCT: A Multidimensional Benchmark and Execution-Free Baseline for Agent Skill Assessment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SkillCT: A Multidimensional Benchmark and Execution-Free Baseline for Agent Skill Assessment
items.summary: arXiv:2610.38147v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills package instructions, scripts, and resources for specialized tasks and are increasingly distributed through public Web repositories. However, existing skill benchmarks primarily focus on downstream task execution, insufficiently assessing specification quality, behavioral robustness, semantic alignment, and responsibility boundaries. Their reliance on task-specific tools, environments, and repeated executions limits scalability and pre-deployment assessment. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillCT, a benchmark that broadens skill assessment from downstream utility to a multidimensional characterization of skill quality. SkillCT evaluates skills across nine complementary dimensions spanning three aspects: Static Assessment, which captures intrinsic properties of the skill specification; Dynamic Assessment, which measures whether the induced behavior remains stable across backbone models and request variations; and Human-Assisted Assessment, which examines behavior-chain consistency and task granularity. These dimensions provide a broader view of skill quality than execution success. Applying SkillCT to a public skill corpus establishes a reference benchmark for analyzing quality weaknesses and relationships across dimensions. Building on this benchmark, we propose an execution-free quality evaluation baseline that predicts the multidimensional quality profiles of unseen skills by retrieving and leveraging similar reference skills, without executing the skills under evaluation. This reduces token consumption and evaluation time, while preserving consistency with the full assessment. Furthermore, SkillCT-guided optimization improves downstream task success and execution efficiency, demonstrating its value for skill refinement. These findings highlight the effectiveness of SkillCT in supporting scalable skill assessment, optimization, and repository maintenance.

items.title: BridgeRouter: Gain-Aware Instance Routing over Cross-Modal Bridge Portfolios [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: BridgeRouter: Gain-Aware Instance Routing over Cross-Modal Bridge Portfolios
items.summary: arXiv:2610.38152v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lightweight representation bridges make pretrained, task-adapted EEG foundation models executable on other biosignal modalities without retraining their backbones. However, selecting a single bridge pathway globally assigns every instance to the same transfer route and ignores complementary errors across routes. We therefore formulate multi-bridge transfer as an instance-level algorithm-selection problem and introduce BridgeRouter, a gain-aware router over a portfolio of frozen cross-modal pathways. A validation-selected Single Best Solver (SBS) serves as a protected default route. During training, task labels are used to compute the reduction in negative log-likelihood provided by each alternative route relative to the SBS, and a lightweight MLP predicts these route-specific gains from a target-modality representation extracted by a frozen encoder. At inference, BridgeRouter observes only the target modality, requires neither EEG, task labels, nor predictions from all candidate routes, and executes exactly one bridge pathway: the route with the largest predicted gain when that gain exceeds a validation-calibrated threshold, and the SBS otherwise. We evaluate seven EEG foundation-model bridge pathways for EMG-based freezing-of-gait detection on FOG and ECG-based sleep classification on ISRUC. Across five seeds, BridgeRouter achieves $81.38\pm1.11\%$ balanced accuracy on FOG, improving over the BIOT SBS by $11.49$ percentage points, and $62.92\pm2.17\%$ on ISRUC, improving over the CBraMod SBS by $3.83$ points. Per-instance bridge oracles reach $99.96\%$ and $78.61\%$, respectively, revealing substantial remaining portfolio headroom. These results show that anchor-relative gain prediction can convert complementary cross-modal bridge behavior into deployable instance-level routing improvements while retaining single-route inference.

items.title: DecompGym: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Designing Decomposition Algorithms [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DecompGym: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Designing Decomposition Algorithms
items.summary: arXiv:2610.38175v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Benders decomposition and column generation solve large optimization problems by passing cuts, columns, and dual values between a master problem and subproblems, and are hard to implement correctly. Large language models now automate parts of algorithm design, which points toward agents that build decomposition solvers for new problems. As a first step toward such agents, we study how well current coding agents design and implement these two algorithms, and how they fail. We introduce DecompGym, 81 instances from nine problem families (five Benders, four column generation), in which an agent writes a solver for a prescribed method. Each solver must meet three criteria: execution within a 60-second time limit; numerical feasibility together with a method audit, in which an LLM judge reads the solver's code; and an objective within 1% of the stored optimal objective. We evaluate 12 GPT, Claude, and Gemini models running in coding-agent tools. Over up to ten attempts, we compare independent regeneration with reflection, which first diagnoses the failure. On the first attempt, two models solve every instance and seven solve more than 90%. Most Benders failures (48 of 62) are missing or suboptimal solutions. The most common column-generation failure is a method-audit rejection. Output checks alone would accept 93 of the 108 attempts that fail the method audit. The most common rejection, an optimalif, occurs 96 times, 92 of them in one model.Reflection turns 66% of retries into successes, compared with 39% for regeneration, and it repairs method-audit failures, for which the judge names the defecective gaps. Agents for decomposition therefore need checks on how a solver reaches its answer and feedback that locates the error. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/SIKAI-C/DecompGym.

items.title: Prototype-Guided Dynamic Domain Modulation and a Large-Scale Multi-SKU Benchmark for Shampoo Bottle Surface Defect Detection [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Prototype-Guided Dynamic Domain Modulation and a Large-Scale Multi-SKU Benchmark for Shampoo Bottle Surface Defect Detection
items.summary: arXiv:2610.38194v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Industrial shampoo-bottle surface defect detection must operate across many stock keeping units (SKUs), where differences in bottle geometry, material, label layout, reflectance, and imaging conditions can substantially alter the appearance of the same defect. Existing industrial defect datasets rarely provide both instance-level defect annotations and product-variant identities, making it difficult to study SKU-aware detection under realistic manufacturing conditions. We introduce Bottle-SKU, a large-scale multi-SKU benchmark for shampoo bottle surface defect detection. Bottle-SKU contains 13,119 images, 20,419 instance-level bounding boxes, seven defect categories, and 48 bottle SKUs, enabling evaluation of both shared defect recognition and SKU-specific appearance variation. To address the challenge of SKU-specific appearance variation, we propose Prototype-Guided Dynamic Domain Modulation (ProDMM). ProDMM constructs a visual prototype for each SKU from training images and predicts a soft SKU distribution for each input. The resulting prototype-conditioned representation dynamically generates low-rank Query/Value modulation for the visual backbone and residual conditioning for defect-text-to-visual attention, while preserving the pretrained Grounding DINO detection pathway. The model is trained jointly with detection, SKU-domain classification, and modulation-regularization objectives. Experiments on Bottle-SKU and the public GC10-DET-SKU metallic surface defect dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of prototype-guided domain conditioning for industrial surface defect detection.
